slide.title: Tests That Run Themselves
slide.body: A branch line joining a main line, with a gate at the join. Red cross on one pull request, green check on another. Small tag: MLOps · Lesson 12.

scenes.voiceover: Your tests from the last lesson are excellent, but they only help if someone runs them. On a busy Friday, someone will forget. Continuous integration runs them for you on every change, and can stop broken code from reaching the main branch.

slide.title: A GitHub Actions workflow
slide.body: Three stacked boxes: Triggers (push, pull request) → Jobs (run on a runner) → Steps (shell command or reusable action). Folder label: .github/workflows/

scenes.voiceover: Continuous integration, or CI, means that every change is tested automatically. We use GitHub Actions. It runs workflows, which are YAML files in a special folder of your repository. Each workflow has three parts. Triggers are the events that start it, such as a push or a pull request.

slide.title: Jobs, runners and steps
slide.body: A clean virtual machine labelled 'runner'. Inside: step 1 check out code, step 2 set up Python, step 3 run a command.

scenes.voiceover: Jobs are groups of steps that run on a runner, a fresh virtual machine provided by GitHub. And each step is either a shell command or a reusable action, such as checking out your code or setting up Python.

slide.title: Our CI job
slide.body: Four steps in a line: install pinned requirements (with pip cache) → python train.py → export_ci_model.py saves model/ → pytest -q with MODEL_URI=model. Side note: the runner cannot see your laptop's mlflow.db

scenes.voiceover: Our CI job installs the pinned dependencies, creates a small model, and runs all the tests. The runner cannot see the MLflow database on your laptop, so CI trains a model and saves it in MLflow format with a two-line script. It caches downloaded packages, so later runs install faster. The pinned requirements from lesson three make that cache reliable and the results repeatable.

slide.title: CI vs branch protection
slide.body: CI alone: runs tests and reports red or green, but merging is still possible. CI plus branch protection: pull request required, red test check means the merge button is disabled.

scenes.voiceover: One more thing. CI alone does not block anything. It only reports. To stop failing code from being merged, protect the main branch. Require pull requests, and require the test check to pass before merging. Now a red check means the change cannot enter main.

scenes.stock_query: boxes moving through factory scanner gate
scenes.voiceover: Think of an automatic safety gate at a factory door. Every box is scanned on the way in. A box that fails the scan is stopped at the door, not found later on a shop shelf.

scenes.stock_query: engineer working on laptop in bright office
scenes.voiceover: Nguyen Thi Lan is a DevOps engineer at a hypothetical travel company in Da Nang, Viet Nam. She adds CI to our wine API. She wants every change tested the same way, whoever makes it.

screen_steps: Open the wine-api repository in the editor
Create .github/workflows/ci.yml with the CI workflow from content.md
Highlight the on: push/pull_request block, then the four steps
Create export_ci_model.py (two lines)
scenes.voiceover: She creates the workflow file and the small export script. The file says: run on pushes to main and on every pull request, use Python three point eleven with a package cache, install, train, export and test.

screen_steps: Commit and push to main
Open the Actions tab on GitHub
Show the ci workflow running
Show the green check mark on the completed run
scenes.voiceover: She commits and pushes to main. In the Actions tab, the workflow starts on a fresh runner. When the run finishes, it shows a green check mark. Every step passed: install, train, export and test.

screen_steps: Open Settings, then Branches (or Rules)
Add a rule for main
Tick 'require a pull request before merging'
Add the required status check: test
Save the rule
scenes.voiceover: Next, she protects main. In the repository settings, she adds a rule that requires a pull request and requires the test check to pass. The menu may be called Branches or Rules, depending on the interface.

screen_steps: Run: git switch -c raise-gate
Change the quality gate to >= 0.90, commit and push
Open a pull request
Show the failing test check and the disabled merge button with its message
scenes.voiceover: Now she tests the gate. She creates a branch, raises the quality gate to zero point nine, commits, pushes and opens a pull request. The test check turns red, and the merge button is disabled because required checks have not passed.

screen_steps: Open the failed job log and highlight the AssertionError from test_quality_gate
Revert the change, commit and push
Wait for the green test check
Merge the pull request
scenes.voiceover: She opens the failed job log and finds the assertion error from the quality gate. Then she reverts the change, pushes again, waits for the green check, and merges. The rule, not a person's memory, protects main.

The common mistake is to put credentials in the workflow file. Everyone with read access can see them, and they stay in Git history, even after you delete the line. Use encrypted repository secrets instead. This CI workflow needs no secrets at all, which is the safest design.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Workflow = triggers, jobs, steps; CI installs, builds a model, runs pytest. 2. Branch protection makes CI a gate. 3. Cache dependencies; no credentials in workflow files.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a GitHub Actions workflow defines triggers, jobs and steps. Our CI installs pinned dependencies, builds a test model and runs pytest. Second, branch protection turns CI into a gate, so pull requests with failing checks cannot be merged. Third, cache dependencies to keep runs fast, and never write credentials in workflow files.

slide.title: Exercise: CI with a gate
slide.body: Push wine-api (no data, models or secrets) · add ci.yml · protect main · blocked pull request screenshot · fix and merge · about 35 minutes

scenes.voiceover: In the exercise below this video, you will push your project to GitHub, with no data files, model files or secrets, add this workflow, protect main, open a pull request with a failing test, and screenshot the blocked merge. Then you fix it and merge. It takes about thirty-five minutes.
Once the tests pass, the next step is to ship. In the next lesson, Building and Publishing Images Automatically, we build and push the image on every merge. See you there.
